core_problem: There is an urgent need to quantitatively evaluate Large Language Models as agents on challenging tasks in interactive environments. Existing evaluation is hampered by the lack of a systematic and standard benchmark for LLM-as-Agent. Prior text-based game environments suffer from closed discrete action spaces and narrow focus on commonsense grounding. Embodied agent simulators are complex multi-modal and do not accurately reflect practical use cases of text-only LLMs. Most benchmarks focus on single environments and fail to provide a comprehensive overview across diverse application scenarios.
methodology_summary: Present AGENTBENCH, a multi-dimensional benchmark consisting of 8 distinct environments to assess LLM-as-Agent reasoning and decision-making abilities. Develop a unified evaluation toolkit for LLMs to operate on diverse customized agent tasks, enabling comprehensive benchmarking of LLM-as-Agent ability. The benchmark is evaluated on 29 different LLMs including both API-based and open-source models.
datasets_eval: AGENTBENCH comprises 8 distinct environments for real-world challenges. Datasets, environments and an integrated evaluation package are released at https://github.com/THUDM/AgentBench. Evaluation is conducted on 29 LLMs, API-based and OSS, across the 8 environments.
empirical_results: Extensive tests over 29 API-based and open-sourced LLMs show top commercial LLMs present strong ability of acting as agents in complex environments, with a significant disparity in performance between them and many OSS competitors no larger than 70B. Typical failure reasons are poor long-term reasoning, decision-making and instruction following abilities, which are main obstacles for usable LLM agents. Improving instruction following and training on high quality multi-round alignment data could improve agent performance. Training on code presents ambivalent impacts on different agent tasks. Overall scores across the 8 environments are reported with average lines for two LLM types.
explicit_limitations: The provided context describes limitations of prior work rather than explicit self-reported limitations of AgentBench: text-based game environments have closed discrete action spaces and primarily narrow focus on commonsense grounding; embodied agent simulators based on games, GUI and indoor scenes are complex multi-modal, do not accurately reflect practical use cases of LLMs, and create a hurdle for urgent evaluation of existing text-only LLMs; most existing agent benchmarks focus on single environments and fail to provide a comprehensive overview of LLMs across diverse application scenarios.
